routes.description: Establish that Christianity can coherently recognize suffering as genuinely wrong within a broken creation while relating it to human freedom, divine presence, justice, and promised restoration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the framework explains why suffering is real evil without requiring a purpose for every tragedy, preserves divine goodness and power, and connects present brokenness to morally adequate divine action and future healing.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account makes coherent overall sense of suffering alongside an all-powerful and all-loving God.

centralBridges.description: Explain how a good creation can be presently broken and why its natural mechanisms can produce suffering without making suffering morally illusory.
Account for divine love through God's presence with sufferers, participation in suffering, and action against evil rather than through a distinct benefit assigned to every tragedy.
Show how resurrection, judgment, forgiveness, and future restoration can heal suffering and put wrongs right without disregarding victims or consequences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground the judgment that suffering and exploitation are objectively wrong rather than merely evolutionarily disfavored.
Explain the roles of consequential human freedom and incomplete present healing within the wider broken-world framework.

routes.description: Establish that suffering is expected under naturalism but creates unresolved tensions among divine omnipotence, perfect love, selective intervention, judgment, and the claimed final defeat of evil.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if apparently gratuitous suffering and the Christian framework's treatment of healing and salvation remain less compatible with an all-powerful, all-loving God than with naturalistic expectations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed reality and distribution of suffering make belief in the specified Christian God unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish why an omnipotent and perfectly loving God would need a morally sufficient account of every evil that God knowingly permits.
Show that natural processes can explain suffering and human aversion to it without invoking divine purposes or transcendent moral explanation.
Test whether selective and ambiguous recoveries provide evidence of divine intervention rather than outcomes expected from natural uncertainty.
Determine whether judgment based on belief or reconciliation treats sincere unbelief and grave wrongdoing consistently with perfect love and proportionate justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether changing Christian moral practice weakens the claimed explanatory advantage of an objective divine standard.
Assess whether promised resurrection and future healing are sufficiently warranted to resolve rather than postpone the evidential problem.

sections.title: Suffering, naturalism, and the coherence of a broken creation
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational clash over whether naturalism adequately accommodates suffering or whether Christian broken-creation claims better explain both its mechanisms and its status as a genuine wrong.

sections.title: Evolution, objective morality, and human dignity
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral aversion, cooperation, objective norms, and equal dignity bear on whether Christianity supplies explanatory resources that naturalism lacks and whether its historical record affects that claim.

sections.title: Divine presence, permitted evil, and future restoration
sections.rationale: The issue tests whether divine solidarity, epistemic limits, resurrection, and eventual healing can reconcile perfect goodness with permitted atrocities, or whether every permitted evil still demands an adequate greater-good justification.

sections.title: Unanswered prayer and evidence of divine healing
sections.rationale: Selective recovery provides a concrete test of the broken-world and partially realized kingdom account against the contention that natural uncertainty predicts the observed pattern better than purposeful divine intervention.

sections.title: Judgment, forgiveness, freedom, and sincere unbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether divine judgment, costly forgiveness, human freedom, and an inclusive invitation can secure justice for victims while treating sincere unbelievers and repentant wrongdoers consistently with perfect love.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Naturalism accommodates suffering as part of nature, whereas divine omnipotence and perfect love imply that every apparently evil event must contribute to a greater good.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Stephen, and the sustained first-person atheist answer occupies the window until the moderator resumes.

response.rationale: This is the opening constructive statement of the principal problem-of-evil route, so no earlier opposing locked move supplies a response target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the debate's central contrast and inferential demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is recoverable, but the universal claim that every evil must yield a greater good lacks a stated modal bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Naturalism's compatibility claim is modest, but the asserted necessity of a greater good exceeds the supplied argument.

charity.alternative: God may permissibly allow evil for reasons other than a benefit produced by each event.
charity.decisiveQualification: Perfect love still requires a morally sufficient permission rationale, even if not an event-specific benefit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if an unstated premise connects omnipotent love to a greater good from every event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The naturalistic contrast is intelligible, but the decisive universal theological implication is asserted rather than defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that suffering makes the specified divine belief unreasonable.

representationalCharity.rationale: The formulation narrows the theistic alternative to event-specific greater goods and omits other permission-based accounts.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says naturalism has no comparable explanatory problem and that Christianity requires suffering to serve a greater good.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: The Christian account of a good but broken creation explains both suffering's natural mechanisms and humanity's conviction that suffering is genuinely wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon directly, and the ensuing extended answer uses her scientific background before the moderator addresses Stephen.

components.text: Why omnipotence and perfect love do not require a sufficient account of every permitted evil

response.rationale: The broken-creation account explains Christian recognition of wrongness but does not address the decisive inference from divine attributes to permitted suffering.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is substantial issue-bearing contrary material, yet it leaves the earlier move's decisive permission demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clear, though the causal and theological content of a world being 'broken' remains underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The framework plausibly accommodates wrongness, but saying it explains the mechanisms and moral status compresses important warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Beauty, brokenness, and moral wrongness are mutually consistent, but the bridge explaining divine permission remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt articulates a coherent framework but supplies little independent support for its broken-creation explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level Christian framework by explaining suffering as real wrong within creation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly presents its own framework and does not materially characterize a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly describes the world as beautiful and broken and validates the judgment that something is genuinely wrong.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolutionary selection explains widespread aversion to suffering and the social impulse to improve conditions through dispositions favoring survival, reproduction, longevity, and prosperity.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen begins after Sharon asks for naturalistic grounds, answers in a sustained first-person explanation, and yields when Sharon responds.

components.text: Whether Christianity is needed to explain humanity's conviction that suffering is genuinely wrong
Whether natural mechanisms can account for widespread aversion to suffering

response.rationale: The evolutionary account directly supplies a rival natural mechanism for aversion, though it does not establish objective moral wrongness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the natural-mechanism component decisively but only partially answers the distinct objective-wrongness component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary proposition is recoverable, but near-universal language about inherited aversion needs ordinary exceptions and scope limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary influence on aversion is asserted at an appropriate explanatory level, with only a bounded implicit scope caveat.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Selection for survival and social functioning provides a coherent explanation of widespread suffering-avoidance dispositions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanism is plausible and representative, but the move compresses verification and does not compare rival cultural explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central naturalistic-explanation bridge by supplying a causal account of moral aversion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers a rival causal explanation without materially reconstructing or weakening the Christian alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes natural selection, inherited social dispositions, and avoidance of suffering in humans and other animals.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Evolution may explain how moral dispositions arise, but it cannot determine why compassionate norms are objectively better than exploitative survival strategies.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon takes the floor in direct acknowledgment of Stephen's evolutionary account and develops the counterargument until Stephen announces his rejoinder.

components.text: Whether evolutionary origins can establish that compassionate dispositions are normatively better than exploitative alternatives

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes causal origins from normative authority and argues that selection alone cannot rank competing survival strategies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts and challenges the decisive inference from evolutionary explanation to moral justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The descriptive-versus-normative distinction is clear, with an implicit limitation to evolution considered without added moral premises.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The inability to derive an objective ranking from a bare causal mechanism is appropriately forceful, subject to an implicit qualification.

charity.alternative: Evolution can explain dispositions while a naturalistic realist supplies independent objective moral truths.
charity.decisiveQualification: The earlier move itself supplied only selection and inherited aversion, not an independent realist foundation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The is-ought distinction is explicit and the alternative-strategy example makes the missing normative premise clear.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual warrant is strong, though the further suggestion that the external standard points toward God remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the upper end of the subsidiary moral-grounding tier by identifying the central normative deficit.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly defeats the evolutionary mechanism as a complete standard, though it does not exclude every naturalistic realism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that multiple survival-conducive moral systems are possible and selection itself cannot declare one objectively better.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Cooperation can be evolutionarily advantageous, while changing Christian treatment of women and slavery weakens the claim that Christianity uniquely supplies unchanging objective moral guidance.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen explicitly introduces his rejoinder, develops both evolutionary and historical objections, and stops as Sharon begins her answer.

components.text: Whether evolutionary cooperation can be favored without supplying an external objective moral standard
Whether Christianity uniquely provides stable objective moral guidance

response.rationale: The move answers with cooperation's adaptive value and a historical challenge to Christianity, but adaptive advantage still does not itself establish objective value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both demands, yet the answer to the descriptive-normative distinction remains materially incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-part argument is recoverable, but 'Christianity' and changing treatment are generalized across diverse texts, eras, and communities.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The historical examples create a serious challenge, but the broad conclusion about objective guidance needs denominational and interpretive qualifications.

charity.alternative: A fixed Christian norm may be progressively recognized while Christian institutions repeatedly violate it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Persistent contrary practice still weakens claims of uniquely clear and reliable historical guidance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical challenge is relevant, but changing practice does not by itself entail a changing underlying divine standard.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Women and slavery are pertinent examples, though their treatment is selective and lacks comparative historical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary moral-history bridge by testing the claimed stability of Christian guidance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The either-God-changes-or-morality-is-not-objective framing underplays progressive recognition and institutional noncompliance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt appeals to expanding empathy and changing Christian positions concerning women, slavery, and transgender people.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity grounds equal human dignity in creation and Jesus's conduct even though later Christian authorities sometimes failed to follow that mandate.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon begins by qualifying Stephen's account and continues through a focused defense of Genesis and Jesus before the moderator intervenes.

components.text: Whether Christianity contains a stable basis for equal dignity despite Christians' changing conduct
Whether historical Christian failures show that the underlying mandate itself changed

response.rationale: The reply identifies Genesis and Jesus as stable normative sources and distinguishes those sources from later failures to follow them.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the historical objection, though it does not fully address every cited practice or interpretive difficulty.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between foundational teaching and later institutional failure is explicit and the equal-dignity claim is stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately limited to a textual and exemplary foundation rather than perfect Christian historical performance.

charity.alternative: Christian institutions' long failures may indicate ambiguity or weakness in the alleged equal-dignity mandate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Institutional failure does not alone prove that the cited creation principle and Jesus's conduct lack egalitarian content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-versus-adherent distinction is valid and supplies a coherent answer to the claim of changing foundational morality.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genesis and Jesus are specific supports, though broader textual tensions and historical interpretation receive limited comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes the subsidiary moral-grounding tier by expressly grounding equal dignity in Christian sources.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges Christian failure while fairly preserving the distinction between a norm and noncompliance with it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts ancient assertions of female inferiority with Genesis's claim that male and female bear God's image equally.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity treats evil as genuinely wrong without requiring each tragedy to be God's will, divine punishment, or a means to a particular benefit.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon for her response, and she gives a continuous answer until the transition to Stephen's interjection.

components.text: The inference that Christianity must assign a particular greater good or divine purpose to every tragedy

response.rationale: The reply expressly rejects the premise that every evil is God's will or an event-specific means and states that Christianity can condemn it without sugar-coating.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies and denies the decisive universal premise, then states the consequence for evaluating tragedy.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes God's will, punishment, resulting goods, and the unqualified wrongness of particular tragedies.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that Christianity need not label each tragedy purposeful is matched to the articulated framework.

charity.alternative: The objection may require a morally sufficient permission reason, not a benefit internal to each tragedy.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting event-specific benefits does not yet answer why a loving omnipotent God permits the event.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinctions are consistent and defeat an event-purpose requirement, though they do not resolve the broader permission problem.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well stated, but support for the wider broken-world theology remains largely internal and asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central permission-of-evil bridge by denying its event-specific greater-good requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly defeats the narrower greater-good formulation but leaves the stronger permission rationale substantially open.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says evil is real and wrong and explicitly denies that suffering must be described as God's will or punishment.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Because an omnipotent and perfectly loving God knowingly permits each evil, Christianity must hold that even apparently gratuitous suffering and atrocities contribute to a superior outcome.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen signals his interjection and restates his logical argument in a continuous passage before Sharon begins her disagreement.

components.text: Whether denying God's authorship or will removes the need for a sufficient reason for divine permission
Whether an omnipotent God could prevent each permitted evil

response.rationale: The reply directly shifts from divine authorship to knowing permission and asks why unlimited power and perfect love would allow each evil.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive distinction and explains why permission, rather than direct causation, preserves the objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The permission argument is clear, but the stronger conclusion that every evil produces a superior outcome lacks an explicit bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A sufficient permission reason plausibly follows, but a greater good produced by every evil is stronger than the stated premises warrant.

charity.alternative: God may have morally sufficient permission reasons involving freedom, regular laws, or global goods without each evil producing a greater good.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such reasons still require defense against apparently preventable horrors and available less harmful alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The permission question follows well, but the transition from sufficient reason to superior event-specific outcome is unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Atrocities make the challenge vivid, yet the crucial modal premise and comparison with alternative permission accounts are undeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It sits at the top of the central permission tier by directly formulating the indispensable con-side challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves a powerful permission challenge but repeatedly treats one contested greater-good model as logically mandatory.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that an all-powerful God can prevent evil, knowingly permits it, and therefore owes an explanation for allowing it.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Some atrocities are unqualified evils rather than necessary means to greater goods, while human inability to identify all divine reasons does not establish that none exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon begins with an explicit disagreement, develops the distinction between evil and resulting good, and completes her epistemic point as the moderator moves on.

components.text: Whether every permitted atrocity must itself contribute to a greater good
Whether inability to identify divine reasons establishes that no sufficient reasons exist

response.rationale: The reply explicitly denies greater goods from genocide and adds an epistemic caution about inferring absence of reasons from human ignorance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive universal claim but only partly answers the deeper demand for a morally sufficient permission account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between resulting good and sufficient reason is not kept fully stable, leaving the exact epistemic claim somewhat unclear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited epistemic point that unknown reasons may exist is appropriately cautious, although its scope is only implicit.

charity.alternative: The objection is evidential: apparently gratuitous evil may lower God's probability without claiming certainty that no reason exists.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mere human ignorance does not by itself neutralize evidential weight from the scale and distribution of suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemic caution is valid, but combining 'no greater good' with possible divine reasons leaves their moral role underexplained.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genocide examples support the moral intuition, while the unknown-reasons response lacks independent constraints or comparative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central permission bridge by denying both event-specific benefits and an inference from ignorance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the logical limit but risks answering a certainty claim stronger than the most reasonable evidential objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls genocide and the Holocaust abject evil with no resulting greater good and invokes limits on human knowledge.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christianity answers suffering through a God who entered history and suffered in Jesus, remains present with sufferers, and promises resurrection and eventual healing.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly directs the Christian-worldview question to Sharon, and the uninterrupted answer uses first-person Christian testimony consistent with her position.

components.text: Why divine presence, suffering, and future healing morally justify God's permission of preventable evil

response.rationale: Solidarity and restoration are relevant divine responses, but the move does not show why they justify allowing each preventable atrocity initially.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies meaningful contrary material about divine response while leaving the decisive permission inference uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-part claim about incarnation, present help, and future resurrection is clearly separated and recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Personal experience supports a modest testimony, but the broader claims of divine presence and restoration exceed that evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Solidarity and promised healing coherently express concern, but they do not supply the missing permission justification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on scripture, doctrine, and personal testimony without independent support for resurrection or universal restoration.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It nearly maximizes the central divine-response tier through explicit solidarity, presence, and restorative action.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily develops a positive Christian response and does not substantially characterize an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites God's presence in trouble, personal Christian experience, Jesus's suffering, and the promise of resurrection and healing.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Christian promises of future healing merit skepticism, and restricting their benefit to believers would treat sincere unbelievers incompatibly with the perfect love attributed to God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks whether heaven is a helpful fiction, after which Stephen gives a sustained skeptical analogy and explicitly speaks from the atheist position.

components.text: Whether promised future healing is warranted and available to sincere unbelievers
Whether exclusive salvation is compatible with perfect divine love

response.rationale: The reply directly questions the truth and scope of future healing and argues that excluding sincere atheists conflicts with perfect love.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the promise's warrant and beneficiary scope, though it compresses variation among Christian salvation views.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but it moves broadly among Christianity, Islam, heaven, hell, belief, and salvation without doctrinal qualifications.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Skepticism is warranted, but the assumed exclusivity and fate of all sincere unbelievers are broader than the evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: Christian accounts may distinguish explicit belief from culpable rejection and may allow inclusive or postmortem reconciliation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move can still demand clarity about who benefits and why sincere nonbelief would warrant exclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If exclusivity and punishment are granted, the love tension follows; the weakness is that those doctrinal premises are insufficiently fixed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to attributed teachings creates a relevant challenge, but doctrinal breadth and future-life claims are not documented comparatively.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central salvation-justice bridge by testing sincere unbelief against perfect love.

representationalCharity.rationale: It raises a serious qualification but treats one exclusivist reading as though it exhausted the Christian alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt questions whether atheists share the promised hope and invokes teachings allegedly limiting heaven to believers.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Final judgment expresses divine love because God knows every heart, corrects earthly injustice, opposes evil, and extends an inclusive invitation to reconciliation.
moves.attributionBasis: The response adopts the Christian first-person plural and directly develops Sharon's recurring claims about ultimate justice, divine love, and an open invitation to God.

components.text: Whether divine judgment and salvation can treat persons justly rather than excluding them merely for sincere unbelief
Whether future restoration corrects rather than merely postpones earthly injustice

response.rationale: The reply stresses divine knowledge of hearts, ultimate justice, opposition to evil, and an inclusive invitation, but does not specify sincere unbelievers' fate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central love-and-justice concern but leaves the decisive application to earnest nonbelief materially incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: Judgment and invitation are clear, but 'radically inclusive' is not defined in relation to belief, opportunity, or final outcome.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical assurance of perfectly loving justice lacks a stated account of difficult cases such as sincere nonbelief.

charity.alternative: An invitation may be formally open while sincere evidential nonbelief prevents a person from accepting it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Perfect knowledge of hearts could matter, but the reply must explain how it changes the unbeliever's final treatment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Love, judgment, and reconciliation can be consistent, but the mechanism connecting invitation to proportionate outcomes remains unspecified.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claims rest mainly on asserted Christian doctrine and do not establish how divine heart-knowledge resolves the hard case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central restoration-and-justice bridge through judgment, opposition to evil, and reconciliation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply affirms inclusion without fully engaging the objection that inability to believe differs from willful refusal.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes final justice, God's concern about evil, love for persons, knowledge of hearts, and a radically inclusive invitation.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Unanswered healing prayer reflects a broken world in which God's kingdom has begun but is incomplete, so non-healing implies neither deficient faith nor divine punishment.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Sharon by name, and her uninterrupted answer explains Jesus' healings, Christian prayer, and the unfinished kingdom from an explicitly Christian standpoint.

components.text: Whether promised future healing is sufficiently warranted rather than merely asserted

response.rationale: The move explains non-healing within an incomplete kingdom and rejects blame of sufferers, but it does not supply warrant for future healing or exclusivity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant to deferred healing but does not contact the earlier move's decisive warrant and beneficiary demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly states what unanswered prayer does not mean and locates it within an incomplete present kingdom.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The exclusions are pastorally clear, but saying non-healing simply means continuing brokenness omits competing causal explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: An inaugurated but incomplete kingdom accommodates mixed outcomes, though accommodation alone does not explain their distribution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account is doctrinally articulated but offers no independent evidence distinguishing partial kingdom from ordinary nonintervention.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary freedom-and-prayer tier by directly explaining present non-healing.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explains its own framework and does not materially portray a developed opposing account of non-healing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects deficient faith, inadequate prayer, and punishment as explanations, instead invoking a still-broken world.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Natural uncertainty can explain selective surprising recoveries, whereas genuine divine healing should also produce clear outcomes such as restored limbs rather than only ambiguous remissions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Stephen, whose answer contrasts atheist naturalism with the Christian healing account and presents a sustained skeptical test for miracles.

components.text: Whether an incomplete kingdom explains selective healing better than ordinary natural uncertainty
Whether divine healing should produce clear outcomes unavailable through spontaneous recovery

response.rationale: The reply identifies the framework's lack of discriminating predictions and states that ambiguous remissions fit natural uncertainty while restored limbs would differ.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the evidential defect, offers a contrasting test, and states the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-versus-miraculous comparison is clear, with an implicit limitation to publicly observable healing claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately argues comparative expectation rather than impossibility and acknowledges uncertainty in medical outcomes.

charity.alternative: Divine healing might be rare, non-coercive, or integrated with natural processes rather than spectacular.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such flexibility reduces the account's predictive discrimination unless independent criteria identify divine action.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative prediction is explicit and the restored-limb contrast directly illustrates the proposed evidential discriminator.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The remission-versus-restoration comparison is concrete, though representative medical rates and case documentation are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It maximally advances the central healing-evidence bridge by comparing rival predictions for observed recovery patterns.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly allows surprising recovery but presses the strongest evidential issue: lack of clear differential outcomes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts ambiguous remissions that sometimes occur naturally with the absence of clear outcomes such as regrown limbs.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Sincere unbelievers cannot force conviction in weak religious claims, so eternally punishing earnest nonbelief is inconsistent with an all-loving God who controls the salvific system.
moves.attributionBasis: Following an audience question about atheists and heaven, the speaker identifies himself as an atheist and develops Stephen's established objection to hell and involuntary disbelief.

components.text: Whether a radically inclusive invitation is meaningful when sincere persons cannot voluntarily produce belief
Whether eternal punishment for earnest nonbelief is compatible with perfect love

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes involuntary conviction from refusal and applies that distinction to the claimed inclusiveness and love of judgment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the unresolved hard case and states why an open invitation alone does not answer it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully limits its case to earnest nonbelievers who investigate yet remain unconvinced by the proposition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Involuntariness is well framed, but eternal punishment and belief-based condemnation are treated as fixed without doctrinal qualification.

charity.alternative: Judgment may concern culpable orientation and conduct rather than bare propositional belief, with God knowing each heart.
charity.decisiveQualification: The prior reply did not explain how sincere inability to believe affects final treatment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If sincere conviction is involuntary and punishment tracks nonbelief, the incompatibility with perfect love follows with one doctrinal premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The phenomenology of involuntary belief is strong, but claims about scripture's origins and universal final treatment are lightly supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It sits at the top of the central salvation-justice tier by isolating the sincere-unbelief problem.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move targets the stated gap fairly, though it assumes a relatively strict exclusivist account of eternal punishment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes earnest investigation, inability to force conviction, weak perceived evidence, and the alleged prospect of eternal mistreatment.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Christian forgiveness does not erase justice: Christ bears evil at great cost, victims remain seen, perpetrators face consequences, and reconciliation includes transformation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon to respond, and the long uninterrupted answer consistently presents Christian doctrines of justice, sin, atonement, forgiveness, and moral transformation.

components.text: How sincere involuntary nonbelief is treated within the proposed system of judgment and reconciliation
Whether forgiveness and salvation disregard victims or consequences

response.rationale: The move substantially explains costly forgiveness, consequences, victims, and transformation, but does not answer the decisive sincere-unbelief demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a major justice component while leaving the selected primary component concerning involuntary belief unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions among forgiveness, atoning cost, consequences, victim recognition, and transformation are clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges limited understanding, but categorical assurances against miscarriages of justice remain doctrinally asserted.

charity.alternative: Forgiving a grave offender may still appear unjust if a decent unbeliever is excluded despite sincere inquiry.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cost, consequences, and transformation answer offender impunity but not the comparative fate of the unbeliever.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Costly forgiveness with consequences and transformation coherently avoids simple impunity, despite the unresolved unbelief comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The internal theological structure is detailed, but its atonement, transformation, and perfect-justice claims remain largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It maximally supports the central restoration-and-justice bridge by explaining forgiveness without erasing victims or consequences.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply gives a serious account of forgiveness yet omits the strongest asymmetry already present in the opposition's case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says Christ bears evil at cost, victims remain seen, perpetrators face justice, and reconciliation entails moral change.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: A system that may save a sincerely converted genocidal offender while condemning a decent but unconvinced atheist reverses proportionate moral outcomes and conflicts with a good God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives the remaining seconds to Stephen, who directly criticizes Sharon's preceding answer and contrasts the fates of a genocidal convert and an unconvinced atheist.

components.text: Whether costly forgiveness and transformation prevent disproportionate outcomes between grave offenders and decent unbelievers
Whether a sincere conversion alone appropriately alters a genocidal offender's final status

response.rationale: The reply directly tests the preceding justice account with a converted genocidal offender and an otherwise decent unconvinced atheist.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the unresolved comparative consequence, though its account of conversion and punishment is simplified.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is vivid, but salvation, conversion, punishment, and atheism are treated broadly without conditions or doctrinal variation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The moral challenge is strong, but categorical claims about what Christianity teaches and what any good God would do overreach.

charity.alternative: Genuine conversion may include repentance and transformation, while judgment may retain consequences and assess more than belief labels.
